metadata.title: Compounding Certain Beta-Lactam Products in Shortage Under Section 503A of the Federal Food Drug and Cosmetic Act

candidates.statement: This guidance describes the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA or the Agency) regulatory 17 and enforcement priorities regarding preparation of beta-lactam oral antibiotic suspension 18 products that appear on FDA’s drug shortage list by a licensed pharmacist in a State-licensed 19 pharmacy or Federal facility. There is currently an acute shortage of amoxicillin oral antibiotic 20 powder for suspension. Amoxicillin oral antibiotic powder for suspension products currently 21 appear on FDA’s drug shortage list. Amoxicillin is widely used for the treatment of bacterial 22 upper and lower respiratory infections in the pediatric population, among other uses. As a result 23 of this shortage, there is an urgent need to increase the supply of these beta-lactam oral 24 suspension products. FDA has received a number of reports related to increased demand for 25 amoxicillin oral antibiotic suspension products in particular. FDA has also received requests for 26 clarification about preparation of compounded versions of those products from FDA-approved 27 tablets and capsules. 28

candidates.statement: One of the conditions in section 503A of the FD&C Act is that each drug product must be 54 compounded for an identified individual patient based on the receipt of a valid prescription order 55 or a notation, approved by the prescribing practitioner, on the prescription order that a 56 compounded product is necessary for the identified patient. 2 If an FDA-approved drug product 57 is on FDA’s drug shortage list, it may be compounded by an outsourcing facility in accordance 58 with section 503B of the FD&C Act or by a licensed pharmacist in a State-licensed pharmacy or 59 Federal facility in accordance with section 503A of the FD&C Act. 3
candidates.context: Compounded drug products are not FDA-approved, which means they have not undergone FDA 45 premarket review for safety, effectiveness, and quality. candidates.statement: In addition to penicillin, all beta-lactam drugs can be sensitizing agents; therefore, cross- 72 contamination between any beta-lactam drug and other drugs could initiate the same types of 73 drug-induced life-threatening allergic reactions that penicillins can trigger. Therefore, any 74 handling of any beta-lactam drugs should be done in a manner to prevent cross-contamination 75 with non-beta-lactam drugs, thereby reducing the potential for drug-induced, life-threatening 76 allergic reactions. 77

candidates.statement: 5 Complete and comprehensive separation refers to a cross-contamination prevention strategy that consists of: (1) the complete physical separation of beta-lactam production area(s) (including separate air handling system(s)) from production areas for other drugs; and (2) additional design and procedural controls for facilities, equipment, material, and personnel that are necessary to support and maintain the integrity of the physical separation (e.g., dedicated equipment; utilities management (waste flow, including the potential for beta-lactam production exhaust to contaminate an adjacent building air intake, vacuum systems); people/material/equipment flow; personnel gowning; decontamination; monitoring containment; testing; compliance with procedures; investigations). Although separate buildings could ensure separation of beta-lactam operations from non-beta-lactam operations, it is feasible for one building to contain a dedicated area for beta-lactam production that is completely isolated and sealed off from the rest of the building. For example, separate entries and exits to the beta-lactam segment of the building would be necessary to ensure comprehensive separation. In the limited cases in which this design concept could be considered, a risk assessment should demonstrate that the design provides as much protection against cross- contamination as is achieved by producing in a separate building.

candidates.statement: As noted above, FDA’s insanitary conditions guidance describes the processing of beta-lactams 98 without complete and comprehensive separation from non-beta-lactam products as an example of 99 an insanitary condition the Agency has observed. However, during the time that beta-lactam 100 antibiotic powder for oral suspension products are on the FDA shortage list (or for such shorter 101 time as FDA may announce by updating or withdrawing this guidance based on evolving needs 102 and circumstances), based on the Agency’s current understanding of the potential for risk of 103 contamination, compounders under section 503A of the FD&C Act that prepare beta lactam oral 104 antibiotic suspension products that appear on FDA’s shortage list without complete and 105 comprehensive separation from non-beta-lactam products should take at least the following 106 minimum steps to mitigate the potential risk of cross-contamination and reduce risk to patients. 107 FDA generally intends to prioritize its regulatory and enforcement actions if the following steps 108 are not all followed when preparing beta-lactam oral antibiotic suspension products that appear 109 on FDA’s shortage list without complete and comprehensive separation from non-beta-lactam 110 products: 111
